output:
# My Grooming Van Almost Caught Fire. Here’s What I’ve Learned So Far.

Last Wednesday, October 28, at around 2:15 in the afternoon, I was in a client’s driveway in Bedford drying a Bernese mountain dog named Moose.

The dryer was on high. Moose was being Moose. It was a pretty normal appointment until I smelled hot plastic.

At first, I thought it was the dryer motor. Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat where my batteries are.

I killed the battery switch, got Moose out through the side door and used the extinguisher a bit. I’m honestly still not sure whether I needed to use it, but I wasn’t going to stand there and wait to find out. Moose came out damp and was absolutely thrilled about the unexpected end to his blow-dry.

Everyone is fine. That’s the most important part.

But my van is off the road for at least three weeks, I’ve cancelled 31 appointments so far, and I’m still trying to process how close this felt. Moose’s mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook. I don’t think I properly thanked her in the moment, so if you’re reading this: thank you. I really needed that.

I want to write down what happened and what the electrician showed me, partly because I know other mobile groomers read this blog, and partly because my friend Tasha is about to pay a deposit with the same person who built my van.

**I am not an electrician.** The electrical details below are what I wrote down from my conversation with Priya at Sackville Marine Electric, along with some basic calculations. They’re here to help you ask questions and recognize things worth getting checked—not to tell you to repair or redesign your own electrical system. Please get a qualified professional to inspect your setup.

## The van and the setup

My van was fitted out in spring 2025 by Darren at Coastline Van Fitouts. I have a 3000-watt inverter and two 200Ah lithium batteries in a 12-volt setup.

For anyone who, like me, has spent a lot more time learning how to get undercoat out of a Bernese than learning about electrical systems: the inverter takes power from the batteries and converts it into the kind of power my equipment uses. The cables between the battery and inverter carry a lot of current, especially when you’re running something power-hungry like a dryer.

My dryer draws approximately 1800–2000 watts on high. Depending on what else is running—including whether the water heater is on—the load on the system can be higher.

At 12 volts, 1800–2000 watts works out to roughly **150–167 amps** if you just divide watts by volts. In real life, the inverter isn’t perfectly efficient, so the battery-side current for the dryer can be higher than that. Other equipment adds more load. Depending on what was running and the actual battery voltage, a figure in the neighbourhood of **150–250 amps** is possible—but that’s a rough range, not a measurement Priya took during the incident.

That was one of the things that really landed for me: a number of watts that sounds ordinary when you’re talking about a dryer can mean a *lot* of current on the 12-volt side.

## What Priya found

The cable from the battery to the inverter was **4 AWG**. Priya told me that for my 3000-watt, 12-volt inverter, it should have been **2/0 cable**.

Cable sizing isn’t as simple as picking a number from someone else’s blog post. It depends on the equipment, cable length, installation and applicable standards, among other things. But for *my* setup, Priya was clear that the 4 AWG cable was not what she wanted to see.

The positive-end lug—the metal connector on the end of the cable—was also badly crimped. Priya said it looked like it had been done with something like pliers or a hammer rather than a proper crimper. Heat-shrink had been covering it, so it wasn’t something I could see just by looking at the outside of the connection.

After the incident, the lug was black, and the cable jacket had melted back about three centimetres.

A poor connection can create resistance, and resistance under a heavy load can make heat. The undersized cable and the crimp were both concerns Priya identified. I can’t tell you precisely how much each contributed or claim to have reconstructed every second of what happened. I can tell you that there was smoke, melted cable and a blackened lug, and that the electrician who inspected it said the main runs need to be rewired.

There was also a **300-amp ANL fuse**, but it was mounted about **90 centimetres from the battery**. Priya told me she would want the protection much closer—around **18 centimetres**, or roughly seven inches, in my case.

The reason that matters, as I understand it, is that the length of positive cable between the battery and the fuse may not be protected by that fuse. The right fuse type, rating and placement depend on the system and the standards being followed, so please don’t treat my numbers as instructions to move or replace yours yourself. Ask the person inspecting your van what protects each main cable and why it’s located where it is.

The repair quote is **$4,200**. That includes rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and a Class T fuse. Parts are on order, and the estimate is at least three weeks off the road.

## The photos I can’t stop thinking about

Priya pulled up my damage photos beside thermal-camera shots of her own van running a similar kind of load. In her photos, the connections barely got warm. In mine, the lug was black and the insulation was melted.

The difference was wild. And it made me realize how much I’d been trusting appearances.

My build looked tidy. The wires were covered, everything had a place, and it looked professional to me. I took that as reassurance.

**Tidy is not the same as right.**

I’m not saying you can tell whether a build is safe by making it look messier, either. I’m saying a neat bench seat and clean-looking wiring don’t tell you whether the cable is sized properly, whether a lug was crimped correctly or whether the fuse is in the right place.

I also had no smoke detector in the back of the van—just the one in the cab that came with it. I’m going to ask the professional working on my van what detection is suitable and where it should go. A detector isn’t a substitute for safe wiring, but I wish I’d thought to ask about one in the workspace.

## What I’d check on my own van now

Please read this bit in the spirit it’s intended. This is a **look-and-make-notes checklist**, not a DIY electrical repair guide.

Before looking around, shut down the equipment and use the normal battery disconnect if you have one. **Turning off a switch does not necessarily make every cable or terminal safe:** batteries, inverter capacitors and other connected circuits can remain live. Don’t open battery cases, remove covers, touch terminals, loosen connections, move fuses or pull cables around. If you can’t see something without doing that, leave it for a professional.

And if you smell burning, see smoke, notice active melting or hear concerning electrical noises, stop using the equipment, get everyone out and away, and call emergency services if there’s smoke or fire. Don’t take the van back into service until it’s been assessed.

With that said, here are the things I’d note down:

### 1. Do you know what’s in your electrical system?

Find whatever paperwork you have and write down:

- Your inverter’s make, model and power rating.
- Your battery type, voltage and capacity.
- The make and model of major equipment you run, including your dryer and water heater.
- Any cable sizes, fuse ratings and installation details listed in the documents.

If you don’t have that information, ask your builder or installer for it. “I have a 3000-watt inverter” is a starting point, not a complete description of the system.

### 2. Can you see any obvious signs of heat or damage?

Without touching or moving anything, look at the parts you can safely see. Make a note of:

- Melted, cracked or discoloured cable covering.
- Blackening or scorching around visible connections.
- Damaged cable protection, or cable rubbing against a sharp edge.
- A lingering hot-plastic or burning smell.

Take photos from a safe distance if it’s safe to do so, and show them to a qualified electrician. Don’t assume everything is fine because the damage looks small—or because you can’t see anything. My bad crimp was hidden under heat-shrink.

### 3. Do you know where your battery disconnect is?

You don’t want the first time you look for it to be when smoke is coming out of a bench. Know where your normal disconnect is and what it does. Ask your installer or electrician to explain what it does **not** isolate, too.

Keep the area accessible. And remember that switching it off is not a guarantee that the whole system is de-energized.

### 4. Ask about the main cables and fuses

This is the part I would hand over to a professional rather than trying to judge myself. Ask them to check:

- Are the battery-to-inverter cables correctly sized for the inverter, cable length and installation?
- Are the lugs and connections appropriate and properly crimped?
- What fuse protects each main cable? Is its type and rating appropriate?
- Is the fuse positioned appropriately near the power source?
- Are the batteries, inverter and protective devices compatible with the loads you actually run?

Have the conversation using your real working setup. Tell them whether you run the dryer on high while the water heater or other equipment is on. A system needs to make sense for how you actually use the van, not just for a lovely empty-van photo.

### 5. Check your safety equipment

Do you have suitable smoke detection in the working area, and is it tested and maintained according to the manufacturer’s instructions? Is your extinguisher appropriate, accessible and in date? Do you know how to get yourself, the dog and anyone else out quickly?

I’m asking my electrician for advice on the right equipment and placement for my van. Your local fire service may also be able to help with general fire-safety questions.

### 6. An infrared thermometer can be useful—but it can’t clear your van

I bought a cheap infrared thermometer for **$40 at Canadian Tire**. It’s one more way to notice an unusual hot spot, but it is **not** proof that a connection or electrical system is safe. Readings can be misleading depending on the surface, angle and settings, and the outside of a connection may not tell you what’s happening underneath.

Please don’t open covers, expose live parts or put yourself near damaged equipment to take a reading. If something seems unusually hot or you have any reason to be concerned, stop using it and get a professional to look. And don’t keep running a system that smells like burning just so you can collect a temperature reading.

## Tasha, this part is for you

I know we’ve already talked, but I want this here for anyone else about to hand over a deposit for a mobile grooming build.

Ask for the **cable sizes and fuse specifications in writing before you pay**. Ask where the fuses will be located, what equipment the system is designed to run at the same time, and who will install and inspect the electrical work. Ask for the inverter and battery details, too.

If you don’t know what the answers mean, that’s okay. I didn’t either. You can take the written plan to a qualified independent electrician and ask them to review it before you commit. I wish I’d done that.

I’m not writing this to trash Darren publicly. Coastline Van Fitouts built my van, and these are the details of what happened and what Priya told me after inspecting it. I’ve sent Darren three texts and an email and haven’t heard back yet. If that changes, I’ll update you. People can make up their own minds.

## Where things are now

Right now, I’m scared and pretty overwhelmed. This van is my whole income. Rent is due on the first, and I’m looking at a $4,200 repair and weeks without being able to work.

I’ve cancelled 31 appointments so far, which feels awful. To everyone who had to rearrange their plans, especially those of you who’ve been so kind about it: thank you. I know your dogs still need their appointments, and I’m sorry I can’t be there as planned.

Insurance has said maybe. The adjuster is coming Thursday, so I should know more after that, although I don’t want to get ahead of myself. For now, the parts are on order and I’m waiting.

I keep coming back to the fact that Moose is okay, I’m okay, and the client’s home is okay. It could have been worse. It was still frightening, and it’s okay to say that too.

If you have a grooming van, please take a little time to find your paperwork and ask questions about your setup. If you’re about to buy a build, get the specifications in writing before the deposit. And if anything smells hot or looks wrong, don’t talk yourself out of taking it seriously the way I almost did when I thought it was just the dryer.

I’ll post again when the van is back and I know more. For now, give your dogs a cuddle for me—including the ones who would rather stay damp.
